newsitem.title: USA: Swiss try to smooth relations with Jews.
newsitem.headline: Swiss try to smooth relations with Jews.

text.p: An embarrassed Switzerland sent a special envoy on Monday to reassure Jews that it will set up a multimillion dollar fund for Holocaust victims despite comments by a top Swiss diplomat that his country was in a public relations "war" with Jews.

The envoy met privately for more than an hour on Monday afternoon with World Jewish Congress President Edgar Bronfman to discuss a fund for Holocaust victims and ways to avoid having Swiss-Jewish relations degenerate into further name-calling and accusations, sources close to the talks said.
The sources called the meeting positive but declined to discuss details.

It came after the State Department and Senate Banking Committee chairman Alfonse D'Amato erupted in anger at the remarks by Swiss Ambassador Carlo Jagmetti that called for "waging war" on the public relations front against the WJC and other critics of Switzerland's Second World War role.

Although the ambassador resigned on Monday, D'Amato called on the Swiss government to repudiate his remarks immediately, saying, "We have heard this language all too often in the not too distant past. It is frightening." The State Department called the remarks troubling and wrong-headed.

Bronfman, in a telephone interview before his meeting with the Swiss envoy, told Reuters he didn't want to comment on Jagmetti's remarks or on a since-repudiated comment by former Swiss President Jean-Pascal Delamuraz in which he accused Jewish groups of blackmail and extortion.

"I'm not going to concern myself with him or his resignation or even with Delamuraz's comments. ... I have never seen a country (whose envoys) go out of (their) way to do stupid things, like ex-president Delamuraz and this Washington ambassador," Bronfman said.

Delamuraz's comments caused protests from Jewish groups and from D'Amato, a champion of Jewish efforts to get Switzerland to account for the millions of dollars deposited in its banks by Holocaust victims.
The ex-president's comments were apparently based on reports of Swiss negotiations with the WJC, the group charged by Israel to seek restitution on behalf of world Jewry.

Swiss negotiators reported that the WJC demanded a $250 million fund for Holocaust victims, but Bronfman and others involved in the negotiations said the figure was one actually proposed by the Swiss.
Plans for the fund were probably being prepared, Bronfman said on Monday.
"Now, I think they are putting it together as we speak... Hopefully, they will do the thing right, and ... it will be great," he said.

Rather than being upset with the controversial remarks, Bronfman said he was worried that such incidents create an "atmosphere where anti-Semites can be screaming and shouting and making a lot of noise.

"I'm not going to panic about this. One of these days I plan to talk to the Swiss people and tell them that we're not mad at them. But still, they should know and we should know the truth of what actually happened."

Jagmetti resigned on Monday after a Swiss newspaper revealed a confidential memo he had written in which he argued that Switzerland should make a payment to silence its critics, but added, "This is a war that Switzerland must wage and win on the foreign and domestic front ... You cannot trust most of the adversaries."
